blocks.q: How much should it cost to paint the interior of a 2,000 square foot house?

a.text: A full interior repaint of a 2,000 sq ft home typically runs $3,800 to $18,000 in this market — generally $3.00 to $7.00 per square foot of floor area for walls, ceilings, and trim.
a.html: A full interior repaint of a 2,000 sq ft home typically runs $3,800 to $18,000 in this market — generally $3.00 to $7.00 per square foot of floor area for walls, ceilings, and trim.

a.text: The variables that move it most are not the ones people expect. Trim and doors take far more labor per square foot than walls, so a home with extensive millwork prices well above a simple one. Ceilings add meaningfully. Color changes — particularly light over dark, or any strong color — often need an additional coat. And wall condition matters: patching, texture repair, and skim coating are separate from painting and should be itemized separately in any honest estimate.

a.text: Most three-bedroom interiors run $3,200 to $6,500 for a full repaint including walls, ceilings, doors, and trim. Individual rooms typically run $600 to $1,200 each depending on size, ceiling height, and trim detail.

blocks.q: Do I need to move out while you paint?

a.text: Almost never. We work room by room so you keep the majority of your home in use throughout, and modern low- and zero-VOC paints mean rooms are typically usable the same evening. It’s recommended you move out if we’re doing mill work or cabinets, or if we’re priming.

a.text: We move and center furniture rather than asking you to empty rooms, cover everything remaining, protect floors on the full path from entry to work area, and clean up at the end of each day rather than only at the end of the project. Occupied homes are the normal case for us, not an accommodation. We do not move electronics or art; they are the responsibility of the owner.

blocks.q: What paint sheen should I use in each room?

a.text: A reliable default: flat or matte on ceilings; low-sheen/matte or eggshell on walls in living areas and bedrooms; eggshell or satin in kitchens, bathrooms, and laundry rooms; semi-gloss on trim, doors, and cabinetry.
a.html: A reliable default: flat or matte on ceilings; low-sheen/matte or eggshell on walls in living areas and bedrooms; eggshell or satin in kitchens, bathrooms, and laundry rooms; semi-gloss on trim, doors, and cabinetry.

a.text: The trade-off is straightforward — higher sheen cleans better and resists moisture, lower sheen hides wall imperfections better. In older Eastside homes with plaster or textured walls, dropping to a lower sheen on walls is often the difference between a surface that looks smooth and one where every flaw catches the light. In a bathroom, go the other way; moisture resistance wins.

blocks.q: How many coats do you apply?

a.text: Two finish coats as standard, plus primer wherever it is needed — bare drywall, patched areas, stains, and any significant color change.
a.html: Two finish coats as standard, plus primer wherever it is needed — bare drywall, patched areas, stains, and any significant color change.

a.text: One-coat coverage claims are a marketing position, not a specification. A single coat over an existing color leaves uneven sheen and inconsistent depth that becomes obvious in raking light. Any bid noticeably cheaper than the others is worth checking on this point specifically: ask how many finish coats are included and whether primer is separate. It is the most common place for a low bid to be low.
